idiom_name: trait algebra + explicitly passed dictionary (GAT-based Monad where effect polymorphism is needed)
implementation_notes: Rust has no higher-kinded types, so two hand-written shapes are used. For a first-order DSL the algebra is an ordinary trait parameterised by the representation type (`trait Sym<R> { fn lit(&self, i: i64) -> R; fn add(&self, a: R, b: R) -> R }`), the program is a generic function with a trait bound, and interpreters are unit structs - the final encoding with no AST. For effect polymorphism the closest substitute is a trait whose associated type is itself generic (`trait Monad { type M<T>; fn bind<A, B>(...) }`), which generic associated types made expressible in Rust 1.65; the dictionary is passed as a generic parameter or a `&impl`. What replaces the classic structure: explicit bounds and dictionary arguments instead of implicit resolution - nothing is inferred, everything is threaded. Justified when the same DSL needs several compiled interpretations; for one interpretation, plain concrete types are simpler.
pitfalls: A GAT-based `Monad` needs `where Self: 'a`-style bounds and lifetime plumbing, and it fights the borrow checker for any carrier that borrows - check whether a concrete effect type is enough before building it.
Without implicit resolution the dictionary must be threaded through every call; returning `impl Trait` hides it so thoroughly that tests can no longer substitute an interpreter.
Monomorphisation compiles the program once per interpreter (code size, compile time), and `dyn Sym<R>` cannot be used where the algebra is generic in R without erasing R as well.
Hand-written interpreter state must be owned: a `&mut self` interpreter serialises the whole program, and an interpreter holding `Rc<RefCell<_>>` moves the race from the compiler to run time.
